# Eyeblink conditioning in unmedicated schizophrenia patients: A positron emission tomography study

**Authors:** Krystal L. Parker; Nancy C. Andreasen; Dawei Liu; John H. Freeman; Daniel S. O’Leary

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Psychiatry, Roy J. and Lucille A. Carver College of Medicine, University of Iowa, Iowa City IA 52242, USA | bDepartment of Biostatistics, College of Public Health, University of Iowa, Iowa City IA 52242, USA | cDepartment of Psychology, University of Iowa, Iowa City IA 52242, USA

## Abstract

Previous studies suggest that patients with schizophrenia exhibit dysfunctions in a widely distributed circuit—the cortico-cerebellar-thalamic-cortical circuit, or CCTCC—and that this may explain the multiple cognitive deficits observed in the disorder. This study uses positron emission tomography (PET) with O15 H2O to measure regional cerebral blood flow (rCBF) in response to a classic test of cerebellar function, the associative learning that occurs during eyeblink conditioning, in a sample of 20 unmedicated schizophrenia patients and 20 closely matched healthy controls. The PET paradigm examined three phases of acquisition and extinction (early, middle and late). The patients displayed impaired behavioral performance during both acquisition and extinction. The imaging data indicate that, compared to the control subjects, the patients displayed decreases in rCBF in all three components of the CCTCC during both acquisition and extinction. Specifically, patients had less rCBF in the middle and medial frontal lobes, anterior cerebellar lobules I/V and VI, as well as the thalamus during acquisition and although similar areas were found in the frontal lobe, ipsilateral cerebellar lobule IX showed consistently less activity in patients during extinction. Thus this study provides additional support for the hypothesis that patients with schizophrenia have a cognitive dysmetria—an inability to smoothly coordinate many different types of mental activity—that affects even a very basic cognitive task that taps into associative learning.

## 1. Introduction

Although previously thought to primarily subserve motor functions, the cerebellum is now identified as an important component of the neuronal circuitry that facilitates the smooth execution, or synchrony, of multiple functions in the healthy brain, including both cognitive and affective functions. Because of the extensive cortical and subcortical distribution of its component nodes, it is a critical structure in the cortical-cerebellar-thalamic-cortical circuit (CCTCC). This distributed circuit was identified using both positron emission tomography (PET) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to study cognitive/affective functions in normal individuals, and it has also been found to be abnormal in patients suffering from schizophrenia. The deficits resulting from damage to this circuit are described as cognitive dysmetria and encompass the wide range of symptoms observed in schizophrenia (Andreasen et al., 1998, 1999; Schmahmann et al., 1999; Schmahmann, 2010).

Associative learning is one of the most basic forms of cognition, and it has sometimes been considered to be a purely cerebellar form of learning. Eyeblink conditioning is a classic form of associative learning, and it has provided one of its most widely used and best-understood models in both humans and nonhuman animals. Classical eyeblink conditioning involves the repeated presentation of a neutral conditioned stimulus (CS, tone) paired and co-terminating with an unconditioned stimulus (US, airpuff to the eye). Initial exposure to paired tone and airpuff trials induces an airpuff-evoked reflexive eyeblink. Following repeated paired presentations, an eyeblink develops that precedes the airpuff. This eyeblink is produced from a learned association between the tone and the upcoming airpuff, and it is therefore considered a conditioned response (CR). Recent imaging studies have extended our understanding of the circuitry involved in eyeblink conditioning by demonstrating that in the human brain eyeblink conditioning activates a larger and somewhat different circuitry than that identified in the animal literature. Not only are the cerebellar activations bilateral, but cortical regions are activated as well. Results from PET in healthy controls indicate positive rCBF peaks in the contralateral cerebellar lobules IV/V throughout all phases of conditioning compared to during unpaired pseudoconditioning, as well as positive peaks in bilateral cerebellum during extinction (Parker et al., 2012). Evidence from both fMR and PET imaging studies have confirmed bilateral cerebellar involvement in eyeblink conditioning in healthy controls as well (Molchan et al., 1994; Blaxton et al., 1996; Schreurs et al., 1997; Cheng et al., 2008). Studies of patients suffering from schizophrenia have also indicated the importance of CCTCC dysfunction as a mediator of cognitive dysmetria, but only a few studies have focused on eyeblink conditioning and associative learning, as the most elemental components of cognitive processing. The results of these studies have been inconsistent. Early work examining eyeblink conditioning in schizophrenia using behavioral measures has suggested that patients condition faster than controls and have a higher percentage of CRs (Spain, 1966; Sears et al., 2000). However, more recent studies have reported the opposite result (Hofer et al., 2001; Brown et al., 2005; Edwards et al., 2008; Bolbecker et al., 2009, 2011) indicating eyeblink conditioning deficits in schizophrenia.

Neuroimaging tools provide an opportunity to examine the neural substrates of abnormalities in associative learning in schizophrenia more deeply. Several investigators have examined eyeblink conditioning in schizophrenia patients, but the details of design have varied, making it difficult to compare findings. There is no consistency in previous reports regarding the number of trials presented (Blaxton: 4–15 trial blocks; Schreurs: 2–20 trial blocks; Molchan: 3–30 trial blocks) (Molchan et al., 1994; Blaxton et al., 1996; Schreurs et al., 1997), making it difficult to interpret the lobular variations. These studies also complete the eyeblink conditioning phase of the experiment before beginning neuroimaging. They have all examined patients who are currently treated with antipsychotic medications, thereby introducing a potential confound. The current study is the first to analyze rCBF during different phases of learning and to study medication-free patients. PET imaging was the chosen methodology for this study because it provides quantitative data for analyzing significant changes in rCBF. In addition, eyeblink conditioning methodology involves a puff of air to the subject’s eye, which can produce large movement artifacts during fMRI. PET scans are less susceptible to these artifacts. The eyeblink parameters used in this study are similar to previous reports with the exception of PET scans following each 15-trial block of conditioning. This allows us for the first time to identify brain areas activated during early, middle, and late phases of learning. These imaging data will answer the important question as to whether as learning occurs less rCBF is recruited to perform the learning.

Another novel aspect of this study is that similar to assessing phases of learning, rCBF associated with three phases of extinction is investigated. Extinction involves the presentation of an unreinforced CS (no US), which, in well-conditioned subjects, results in the persistence of CR expression. However, following repeated unpaired presentations, all responses disappear. Studies indicate that extinction engages similar brain sites as those necessary for acquisition, but the results in schizophrenia have been inconclusive. Two studies in healthy volunteers investigated extinction, and while one found no significant cerebellar peaks (Molchan et al., 1994), the second study (from the same group) reported a significant peak in rCBF in the contralateral cerebellar lobule VIII (Schreurs et al., 1997). The experimental design used in these studies consisted of tone-alone extinction where rCBF produced during pseudoconditioning was subtracted. This design fails to control for the US/UR specific activity present during pseudoconditioning. We improved upon this design by following each phase of extinction with imaged pseudoconditioning trials. This allows subtraction of the original pseudoconditioning phase (before any learning/extinction) from the pseudoconditioning phase immediately following extinction. Results of this subtraction indicate extinction-dependent peaks in rCBF.

## 2. Methods and materials

### 2.1. Subjects

Twenty subjects with schizophrenia were recruited through the University of Iowa Mental Health Clinical Research Center (MHCRC). All subjects had a diagnosis of schizophrenia based on the DSM-IV (American Psychiatric Association 1994) and structured interview with the Comprehensive Assessment of Symptoms and History (CASH; Andreasen et al., 1992). All subjects were studied while medication free, having been recruited while they were neuroleptic naïve (n = 5) or having been taken off medications for 3 weeks while in the MHCRC setting. Twenty healthy volunteers were screened using an abbreviated version of the CASH to rule out a history of psychiatric disorder. The control and patient groups were comparable in gender (control = 10 males, 10 females; patients = 11 males, 7 females) and age (control group age, 29.2 ± 9.22 years (mean ± standard deviation), range = 20–48; patients group age, 28.17 ± 9.24 years, range = 18–48. All subjects had normal hearing (based on a hearing screen), no identified neurological abnormalities, and 19 of the 20 subjects in each group were right-handed. Clinical symptoms were assessed using the Scale for the Assessment of Positive Symptoms (SAPS) and the Scale for the Assessment of Negative Symptoms (SANS) (Andreasen, 1983, 1984). All subjects were evaluated with a comprehensive cognitive battery administered by trained neuropsychologists. In order to provide comprehensive measurements of cognitive functioning, 36 neuropsychological test variables (see Supplemental Material for a complete list) were grouped into six cognitive domains: verbal learning, attention, problem solving, working memory, verbal fluency, and motor speed (Andreasen et al., 1992).

### 2.2. Eyeblink conditioning

For eyeblink conditioning, subjects wore headphones for delivery of the tone conditioned stimulus (CS: 75 dB, 1-kHz) and eyeglasses equipped to deliver the air puff unconditioned stimulus (US: 5 psi) to the left eye. The eyeglasses also contained an infrared photo beam system for recording eyeblinks. Stimuli presentation was computer controlled and the eyeblink response, recorded as eyeblink amplitude, latency, and peak, was digitized and stored for subsequent analysis (SanDiego Instruments Eyeblink Conditioning System™). Subjects were given a session of pseudoconditioning to gather baseline information which involved unpaired (UP) tones and airpuffs for a total of 10 trials with 5 CS and 5 US alone. A total of 45 paired CS/US trials were presented to the subjects during the acquisition phase of the experiment. These trials were divided into three 15-trial phases of conditioning—early, middle, and late. PET imaging was performed for the last five trials in each block (see Section 2.4). The tone CS was presented for 500 ms and co-terminated with the 100-ms US producing a 400-ms interstimulus interval (ISI) for eyeblink conditioning. The interval between the trials ranged from 8 to 16 s (M = 12 s). Following the 45 acquisition trials, subjects received 90 extinction trials consisting of three 30-trial phases of extinction—early, middle, and late. In each 30-trial phase of extinction, 20 CS-alone trials were given and then PET imaging was performed for the last 10 pseudorandom trials, 5 CS and 5 US-alone trials.

### 2.3. Behavioral analyses

A CR was counted if the eyeblink amplitude exceeded 10% of the subject’s baseline UR amplitude (based on the mean UR amplitude for 10 US-alone trials presented prior to acquisition trials) and if the eyeblink response occurred between 200 and 400 ms after the CS onset. Eyeblinks fitting this criterion were encoded as a CR and those occurring after 400 ms were encoded as a UR. CR percentage and CR onset latency were then calculated for the responses. In addition, overall eyeblink onset time was calculated for all trials included in the experiment. Eyeblinks occurring prior to 200 ms after CS onset were counted as “alpha” responses (i.e., short-latency, tone-evoked nonassociative responses). Trials where an alpha response was present were excluded from data analysis.

CR incidence was modeled as a binary outcome (yes/no) and onset time was modeled as a continuous outcome. Since each subject was tested multiple times under varying experimental conditions, repeated measurements of CR incidence and onset time obtained from the same subject were correlated. Linear regression or analysis of variance models are not well suited for analysis of correlated data. Therefore, a generalized estimating equation modeling was applied in the analysis of CR incidence and onset times (Zeger et al., 1988; Burton et al., 1998). For both analyses, experimental phase, age, and sex were included as covariates, and the interaction between subject type and experimental phase was also included in the model. The first order autoregressive variance-covariance structure (AR(1)) was used, based on model selection criteria, to model the correlation between repeated measures from the same subject. Linear contrasts of interest on the variable experiment phase were performed to test for relevant hypotheses. A significance level of 0.05 was used for any hypothesis testing reported in this article. All statistical analyses were carried out with SAS v9.2 (Cary, NC). Age over 40 is known to significantly impair eyeblink conditioning; however, age as a covariate revealed no significant effect in this sample (Woodruff-Pak, 1988).

### 2.4. PET imaging

Methods for acquisition and processing of the [15O]water PET imaging data have been previously described (Hurtig et al., 1994). PET data were acquired after the bolus intravenous administration of [15O]water (50 mCi) using a GE 4096-plus whole-body scanner. A preliminary scout injection provided an initial estimate of the bolus arrival time which was then utilized to optimize the timing of imaging (Hurtig et al., 1994). Imaging of the last five trials of each phase of acquisition and extinction was timed to start 10 s before the arrival of the [15O]water bolus in the brain. Images were acquired in 20 5-s frames. Based on time-activity curves over major cerebral arteries, the eight frames reflecting the 40 s after bolus transit were selected and summed (Hurtig et al., 1994; O’Leary et al., 1996). The summed image was reconstructed in 2-mm voxels in a 128 × 128 matrix using a Butterworth filter (expressed in PET counts). Injections were repeated at approximately 15-min intervals (Andreasen et al., 1995a, 1996). MR scans were obtained for each subject with a standard T1-weighted three-dimensional SPGR sequence on a 1.5 T GE Signa (General Electric, Milwaukee, WI) scanner (TE = 5, TR = 24, flip angle = 40, NEX = 2, FOV = 26, matrix = 256 × 192, slice thickness 1.5 mm).

### 2.5. PET image analyses

The anterior-posterior commissure (AC-PC) plane was identified and used to realign the MR images of all subjects to a standard position. The PET image for each subject was fit to their MR scan with AIR (Woods et al., 1998). Images from each injection were checked for head movement and individually re-fit as needed (Cizadlo et al., 1994; Talairach and Tournoux, 1988). To reduce anatomic variability, the PET images were normalized, then smoothed with an 18-mm Hanning Filter (Arndt et al., 1995). An average MRI was generated by transforming the 20 controls and 20 patients’ MR images into a Talairach bounding box. The PET images were brought to standardized space using the transform from the MRI. Analyses for within-group statistical significance were performed using an adaptation of the method of Worsley (Worsley et al., 1992; Arndt, et al., 1995; O’Leary et al., 1996). These analyses included controlling for baseline by subtracting unpaired rCBF from each group. Significant within-group differences were then compared to a between-group double subtraction using a randomization method that has previously been described (Arndt et al., 1996). The double subtraction involved first subtracting the unpaired rCBF associated with patients and controls and then subtracting the patients from the controls (patients-unpaired)-(controls-unpaired). Within-subject subtractions of normalized count images for each phase of the experiment were contrasted via randomization to compute the between-group, voxel-by-voxel p-value. The t-threshold was adjusted to correct for the large number of voxel-by-voxel t-tests performed, the lack of independence between voxels, and the resolution of the processed PET images (Andreasen et al., 1995a, 1995b; O’Leary et al., 1996). Results were visualized overlying the group’s averaged MR scans (Andreasen et al., 1995a).

This study analyzed rCBF during six basic subtractions: early, middle, and late phases of acquisition and extinction with unpaired tone and airpuff-specific activity (pseudoconditioning control task) subtracted. In these analyses, significant changes in rCBF are labeled as positive peaks (greater activity in the experimental task) or negative peaks (greater activity in the control task). Tabled data report the brain regions (nomenclature according to Schmahmann et al., (1999)) with significant changes in rCBF. Individual significant peaks are reported with their corresponding three-dimensional (Talairach and Tournoux, 1988) coordinates (x,y,z), corresponding Brodmann area (BA) when appropriate, size (cc), and the highest t-value (t-max – representing the ‘peak’). Included peaks contain at least 50 continuous voxels that have a t-value threshold of greater than 3.0 (p = 0.005). Talairach coordinates are used to indicate side of the brain in standard radiological convention.

## 3. Results

### 3.1. Eyeblink conditioning behavioral data

Following repeated paired-presentations of the tone and airpuff trials, controls and patients both showed an increase in CR incidence (Fig. 1a, CR Incidence – Conditioning). Specifically, the incidence of CRs for controls increased from 40.97 ± 8.21% (mean ± standard error of the mean) during the early acquisition phase to 64.45 ± 6.28% in the middle whereas patients expressed 28.56 ± 7.26% during early acquisition and 41.01 ± 7.81% in the middle. Although the level of learning asymptotes, the trend of controls expressing more CRs than patients persists during late conditioning (controls: 66.49 ± 5.77%, patients: 43.80 ± 8.78%). Although the early phase did not show significant differences between groups, the middle (z = 2.26, p = 0.024) and late (z = 2.22, p = 0.026) phases of learning revealed significantly more CRs for controls than for the patients.

As a result of learning, eyeblink onset timing decreased representatively for both groups (Fig. 1b, Eyeblink Onset – Conditioning). Controls’ eyeblinks decreased in onset latency during each phase of conditioning (early: 372.74 ± 21.86 ms; middle: 331.61 ± 20.20 ms; late: 312.77 ± 17.03 ms) while patients’ onset latency decreased during the early phase of conditioning (360.75 ± 48.82 ms) and then dramatically increased during the middle phase (375.90 ± 53.38 ms) before decreasing again during late conditioning (353.25 ± 55.80 ms). Interestingly, there were no significant differences in latency between patients and controls at any phase of conditioning. This is likely due to the large variability in response timing in patients. Analyses of CR onset latency as opposed to overall eyeblink onset revealed no significant differences between patients and controls.

### 3.2. Eyeblink extinction behavioral results

Following conditioning, CS-alone trials produced rapid CR extinction for both controls and patients, although the two groups did not differ significantly (Fig. 1a, CR Incidence – Extinction). Controls’ expressed 66.49 ± 5.77% CRs during late acquisition which dramatically declined to 25.67 ± 5.95% during early extinction and continued to decrease into the middle and late phases (Fig. 1a: 21.26 ± 4.81 & 19.33 ± 4.77%). Patients’ expressed 43.80 ± 8.78% CRs during late acquisition which dramatically declined to 15.26 ± 3.88% during early extinction and remained low during the middle and late phases (middle: 11.88 ± 3.72%; late: 14.27 ± 4.42%).

As CR expression decreased due to extinction, eyeblink latency increased (Fig. 1b, Eyeblink Onset – Extinction). During the last phase of conditioning, controls’ CRs occurred with a latency of 312.77 ± 17.03 ms, which increased to 418.31 ± 21.94 ms following early extinction (middle: 378.91 ± 16.36 ms, late: 408.71 ± 15.48). For patients, CR onset latency decreased from 353.25 ± 55.80 ms to 425.56 ± 44.70 ms after the first phase of extinction (middle: 430.19 ± 43.96 ms, late: 400.50 ± 43.96).

### 3.3. Imaging results

PET imaging revealed major changes in rCBF during eyeblink classical conditioning that significantly differed between schizophrenia patients and controls. Changes in rCBF that exceeded our significance level of 0.005 are reported as negative (less than −3.0) peaks in rCBF that vary in location as acquisition and extinction occur. The two tables show CCTCC brain areas with relatively less rCBF in schizophrenia patients (Table 1: acquisition, Table 2: extinction). The tables are organized by three phases (early, middle, and late) of conditioning/extinction, and all conditions control for pseudoconditioning by subtracting stimuli-specific activity from each phase of the experiment. Within-group Tmax values are also included in the table to interpret the direction of each peak in rCBF. Using the Talairach coordinates from the between-group subtractions, the Tmax values for the identical locations in patients and controls are listed for each significant peak at each phase of the experiment. Ipsilateral localizations are identified by peaks with a negative x-Talairach coordinate, which indicates the left side of the brain, and contralateral localizations are identified by a positive x-coordinate indicating the right side (the left eye was conditioned with the airpuff). Subtracting the patient T max values from the controls indicates whether there was quantitatively less rCBF in patients than controls at each phase of eyeblink conditioning and extinction.

#### 3.3.1. Acquisition

During eyeblink acquisition, many significant differences in rCBF between schizophrenia patients and controls are revealed by the randomization analysis (Table 1). These differences were consistently found in the frontal lobes, thalamus, and cerebellum.

One of the main findings in this study is hypofrontality in patients with schizophrenia in comparison to controls (Fig. 2). Patients have decreased rCBF in multiple regions in the frontal lobes. The contralateral medial frontal gyrus, BA 10, had negative peaks during all phases of eyeblink conditioning whereas BA 25 peaked during middle and late conditioning. There was also an ipsilateral medial frontal negative peak at BA 11. The second major location in the frontal lobe showing less activity in patients than controls was the contralateral middle frontal gyrus (BA 8 and 11 during early; BA 10 during middle).

Furthermore, patients also show hypocerebellar functioning during acquisition. The between-group randomization revealed that patients have significantly less cerebellar activity than controls during all three phases of conditioning (Fig. 2). Negative peaks were found in contralateral cerebellar lobules IV and V indicating that patients have less rCBF than controls. In addition to lobules IV and V, late acquisition showed less rCBF in patients than controls in posterior ipsilateral cerebellar lobule VI. The thalamus showed decreased flow during early and late acquisition; a similar pattern was noted during middle acquisition, but it did not reach our significance threshold.

Other brain regions also showed decreased flow in patients during acquisition; these locations can be found in Table 1.

#### 3.3.2. Extinction

Extinction also revealed dynamic rCBF differences between schizophrenia patients and controls in the frontal lobes, thalamus, and cerebellum (Table 2).

Similar to during acquisition, all phases of extinction revealed less rCBF in patients than controls in the medial and middle frontal gyri. BA 10 in the medial frontal gyrus had negative peaks during all three phases of extinction (Fig. 2). During early extinction the peak in BA 10 was located contralaterally while during middle it was ipsilateral and then during late extinction there were bilateral peaks. Similarly, BA 8 showed less rCBF in patients than controls during early (contralateral) and middle (ipsilateral) conditioning.

During all phases of extinction, within-group analyses revealed hypocerebellar functioning in patients while the controls showed increased blood flow in similar lobules (Fig. 2). The between-group comparison corroborated this abnormal hypocerebellar functioning by revealing negative peaks in lobules IV/V during middle and late extinction. In addition, less rCBF was found in lobules IX during all three phases of extinction. Late extinction also revealed several peaks with less rCBF in patients in lobule VI. The thalamus showed decreased flow only during early extinction.

Other brain regions also showed decreased flow in patients during extinction; these locations can be found in Table 2.

### 3.4. Relationship with clinical and cognitive measures

We examined the relationship between impairments in eyeblink conditioning and clinical and cognitive measures by calculating the correlation coefficients between severity of positive and negative symptoms and the behavioral measures for the three phases of acquisition and extinction. We also calculated the coefficients between scores on the six cognitive domains and the phases of acquisition and extinction. During early conditioning, scores on language tests (r = 0.71871, p = 0.0084) and motor skills (r = 0.60651, p = 0.0365) showed that the better the subjects’ language and motor skills, the more likely their eyeblinks were to have longer, more appropriately timed onset times. Negative symptom severity (r = −0.56318, p = 0.0360) and motor skills (r = −0.57185, p = 0.0412) were negatively correlated with poor performance during extinction (middle extinction for motor skills and late for negative symptom severity); that is, the worse the negative symptoms and motor skills, the less likely they were to extinguish the previously learned eyeblink responses.

## 4. Discussion

In the present study we examined the CCTCC/cognitive dysmetria hypothesis by studying schizophrenia patients using the most classical test of cerebellar function: the associative learning that occurs during eyeblink conditioning. We compared changes in rCBF during three phases of eyeblink conditioning and extinction in schizophrenia patients and healthy controls. Known for its reliance on normal cerebellar functioning, eyeblink classical conditioning was chosen as a behavioral indicator for cerebellar integrity. We hypothesized that patients with schizophrenia would show impairments in eyeblink conditioning and that they would be associated with rCBF abnormalities in the cerebellum, as well as other components of the CCTCC.

The data presented here support our hypothesis and show that patients with schizophrenia have a deficit in eyeblink conditioning as shown in Fig. 1b, CR incidence. Eyeblink conditioning is significantly impaired in the patients, and they exhibit significantly fewer CRs during the latter two phases of acquisition than controls. These data replicate previous studies reporting abnormalities in eyeblink conditioning in schizophrenia patients (Brown et al., 2005; Bolbecker et al., 2009, 2011). However, the onset timing of both the overall eyeblink and the CR was non-significant (Fig. 1a), which is likely caused by the small sample size and large variability in the response onset. While healthy controls develop a learned eyeblink response appropriately preceding the airpuff, this learned timing component is altered in patients producing large variability in eyeblink onset.

Our PET data permit us to examine the neural substrates of the behavioral impairments. While we cannot definitively determine the directionality of the results (i.e., whether the behavioral abnormalities are due to brain abnormalities, or whether poor task performance leads to the activations seen via PET imaging), our previous work implicating CCTCC abnormalities and cerebellar dysfunction during normal task performance, suggests that the brain abnormalities may be primary. The between-group randomization results indicate that all of the areas showing significant differences were a result of the opposite pattern of results in controls and patients (i.e., when controls showed increased rCBF, patients showed decreased rCBF). This indicates a significant difference in the brain function of schizophrenia patients. We previously reported that right cerebellar lobules IV/V recruit more rCBF during eyeblink conditioning than during unpaired pseudoconditioning (Parker et al., 2012); the results presented here reveal that patients have significantly less rCBF in these same lobules.

However, the cerebellum is not the only brain region exhibiting abnormalities. In the normal brain, eyeblink conditioning recruits increased rCBF in the frontal lobules (Parker et al., 2012) while schizophrenia patients show the opposite pattern of results and less rCBF is recruited with several negative peaks in the frontal lobes. These results indicate hypofrontal activity during all phases of conditioning. The areas of decreased rCBF in the frontal lobes show dynamic fluctuations between Brodmann locations although the majority of the peaks were located within the contralateral medial and middle frontal lobules. All of the brain regions are known to be involved in higher order processes. For example, BA 10 showed consistently decreased rCBF throughout all phases of learning and is known to be involved in strategic processes of memory retrieval and executive function (Rasser et al., 2005). In addition, BA 11 is known to function in planning, reasoning, and decision making (Shurman et al., 2005), while BA 47 is involved in syntactical processing (Dapretto and Bookheimer, 1999). These contralateral frontal decreases may directly correlate to the decreases in cerebellar activity as the cerebellum projects to the contralateral frontal lobules (Middleton and Strick, 2001).

Tone-alone extinction yielded an interesting pattern of peaks in rCBF. Following acquisition, initial presentation of tone-alone extinction trials continued to elicit CRs but following repeated presentation CRs decreased and both patients and controls extinguished. As previously described for healthy adults, extinction involves active loss of CRs due to context-dependent (presence of the CS and US) inhibitory learning (Parker et al., 2012). The learned-association between the tone and airpuff remains, which is supported by reports of faster reacquisition and immediate restoration of CRs following subsequent CS & US paired presentation (Falls, 1998; Robleto et al., 2004). The experimental design used by our study involved each block of extinction followed by imaged unpaired tone and airpuff pseudoconditioning trials. One downside to this design is incomplete extinction due to the attempt to re-associate once the airpuff is reinstated. As a consequence the 30 extinction trials (double that presented during conditioning) were presented for three phases to allow for the most complete extinction before each imaging session. This design allowed subtraction of the original pseudoconditioning phase (before any learning/extinction) from the pseudoconditioning phase immediately following each phase of extinction. These data indicate extinction-related abnormalities in the CCTCC similar to during acquisition but with some variation. For example, cerebellar lobules IV/V are consistently recruited during acquisition and although these lobules are also recruited during middle and late extinction, lobule IX showed significantly less rCBF in patients than controls during all phases of extinction. This provides evidence that acquisition and extinction are separate processes but they both rely on the proper functioning of the CCTCC.

Several cognitive/clinical impairments in schizophrenia were highly correlated with eyeblink expression/timing. Specifically, patients with better language capabilities showed faster eyeblink conditioning than those who had impaired language skills as shown by more conditioned responses during the early phase. Although language is known to involve Brodmann areas 44 and 45, these areas did not show significant between-group rCBF differences in our study. Therefore, it is possible that the reported hypocerebellar activity contributes to these impairments as cerebellar activation has been implicated in language (De Smet et al., 2007). Patients with better motor skills also learned faster but did not show better overall performance as indicated by non-significant correlations in the last two phases of learning. This result is fairly straightforward in that the cerebellum is essential for motor control, the cerebellum is hypoactive in schizophrenia, therefore combined with impaired motor skills, patients take longer to condition in this motor learning task. In addition, the more negative symptoms a patient has, the less efficiently they extinguish during the last phase. These negative symptoms result from abnormalities in the CCTCC and included flattened affect, alogia, avolition-apathy, anhedonia-asociality, and attentional impairment (Andreasen, 1983). Taken together, these data indicate that proper communication in the CCTCC is necessary for eyeblink conditioning and extinction, which are critically affected by impaired language capabilities, motor skills, and the presence of negative symptoms in schizophrenia.

We have previously conducted studies that have examined the functionality of the CCTCC in patients suffering from schizophrenia and have found it to be disrupted in a variety of different tasks, thereby suggesting that the illness involves a cognitive dysmetria—a problem in smoothly coordinating mental activity that leads to the generalized cognitive deficits that are observed in schizophrenia (Andreasen et al., 1996, 1998, 1999). Our earliest report of PET data supporting the concept of cognitive dysmetria derived from our studies of recall memory for complex narrative material (Andreasen et al., 1995a, 1995b). When we studied patients with this memory task, we equalized task performance in patients and controls by providing the patients with multiple practice sessions prior to the PET study, thereby permitting them to achieve near-perfect recall (Andreasen et al., 1996). We concluded that any observed abnormalities were due to primary abnormalities in circuitry, rather than to the secondary effects of poor task performance. Thereafter, we examined a variety of additional tasks and extended our exploration to include practiced and novel recall of word lists (Crespo-Facorro et al., 1999), recognition memory for word lists (Wiser et al., 1998), recognition memory for faces (Wiser et al., 2000), hedonic capacity using visual stimuli and olfactory stimuli (Crespo-Facorro et al., 2001), and directed visual attention (O’Leary et al., 1997). All of these studies were conducted with unmedicated patients, thereby eliminating the potential confounding effects of antipsychotic medications. Cerebellar and frontal dysfunctions were found in all of these studies and thalamic dysfunction in the majority, thereby suggesting that schizophrenia is characterized by a “misconnection syndrome” in distributed brain circuitry.
